title: How can I properly rig, animate and equip a meshy model?
author: luka_makes_games
selftext:
Hey people!

I've been trying this all that, AI can't get it right. I meshed a Meshy model, rigged it in mixamo and download an idle stance with the rigged mannequin. My AI has restlessly tried equipping it and animating weapon stances, but no matter what Fable does, it always gets it wrong.

Out of all things AI does great, for some reason it just cannot get this right.

I would love to hear all tips & ideas here! Greatly appreciated.

Cheers

comments.author: TechnicSonik
comments.body:
You can rig directly in Meshy aswell. 

The best flow i ve found so far is 

1) Basic Rigging on Meshy  
2) Get the Blender MCP and use Opus 5 (Be ready to burn alot of tokens)

comments.author: AlarakReigns
comments.body: Cascadeur is extremely useful Im using it for my game. Do not use blender, it will take you likely 24-48 hours of animation practice to get a good hang of it, look up a video of how the ai can do the work for you after you make a pose. Using tokens will take you 10x the length. If your game doesnt care about weapons having its own bones then you can ask claude to make a prop fitter if you plan on weapons being interchangeable in poses, it will save you a lot of time once you understand the pose you are looking for.  Casc is very cheap and you will be able to do a lot of what you need and see results fast, The only reason it takes longer in the start is if you have 0 experience, but touching up in blender will likely take way longer with claude than you just practicing cascadeur for a few days.  You can practice using casc for free, but wont be able to export the models into a game or blender until paying the subscription. It has an auto rig tool as well, but usually yoy have meshy rig first then cascadeur will convert it for itself.

comments.author: Lonely-Magician-2704
comments.body:
Il mio consiglio:
1. Genera il modello
2. Caricalo in Mixamo
3. Scarica il t-pose del modello riggato (ti sarà utile in caso di modifiche su mesh, pesature del rig, texture e altro.)
4. Scarica le animazioni che ti interessano "senza skin (senza mesh)" perché come mesh utilizzerai quella del t-pose.(Le altre animazioni saranno interpolate attraverso l'animator se fai giochi) Se non fai giochi e devi fare scende di animazione su Blender o altri strumenti allora ti consiglio di scaricare l'animazione con skin. 

Deduco che ti serva per un gioco.
5. Sia se utilizzerai Unity3D come ambiente di sviluppo o Blender per altro, o qualsiasi altro strumento che usi, dovrai mettere la spada come figlio dell'osso della mano destra o di quella sinistra.
6. Su Mixamo esistono già animazioni adatte a spade a due mani o ad una mano. Se nel momento dell'utilizzo vedi le dita storte è arrivato il momento che impari a pesare le ossa.
Ovvero, negli strumenti come Blender o Cinema4D(quello che utilizzo io da una vita), c'è lo strumento pesa ossa, selezionano qualsiasi osso puoi colorarlo con una sfumatura di peso, più la percentuale di peso è alta più quella parte di mesh collegata a quell'osso sarà interessata. Non riesco a spiegarlo in parole più semplici. Ti consiglio di imparare almeno il concetto di pesatura. Una volta pesate bene le ossa delle dita vedrai che quando in animazione chiuderà il pugno o lo aprirà sarà molto più naturale.

Spero di essere stato chiaro e che ti sia utile a te e ad altri.

comments.author: Xynth22
comments.body:
Don't know what engine you are using, but with some trial and error I know that Opus 5 can do this within Godot. Spent a while fighting it with it to get it right, but I eventually got there.

For me I had my model without animations, but it did have a well set up skeleton. I then downloaded animations in the FBX format. And then had Claude connect everything in Godot, using the built in retargeting tool. It gets pretty close the first time, but there are bones that it won't get right. For me that was the spine, hands, and feet. But with some trial and error, reference pictures of what it should look like, and being very specific, it eventually got it perfectly. 

Though I found that it also helps to start with a more fresh project when working on animations, as Claude seemed to have gotten overwhelmed when I tried adding in a second set of animations on the first project I was testing out animations on, since I had been working on a lot of other stuff prior to that. And then Claude can just copy/paste what works from the animation specific project into your main project after the fact.

comments.author: AliAlHamwi
comments.body:
The weapon part was answered right above, parent it to the hand bone in engine, fit it once, and reuse the offset for every weapon after.

The rigging pain is a different animal. That pipeline is dying at the seams, not at the steps. Generating in one tool, rigging in Mixamo and keyframing with an LLM in a third means every export between them is a chance for skinning, orientation and scale to break silently, and then the LLM catches the blame for damage done two handoffs earlier. Fewer seams beats better steps. Meshy rigging where you generate, as someone said above, is one way to cut a seam. Cutting the same seam is why Ludo.ai's 3D generator now does one-click rigging with animation presets in the place the model was generated, and I work on Ludo, so that recommendation comes from the inside. Either route, do only the last mile in engine.

Also worth one evening of your life: basic weight painting. Fixing finger weights by hand beats fifty regenerations of the whole character.
